title: Hosea 5:1–7
context: The LORD summons three groups at once: the priests, the house of Israel, and the house of the king (5:1). Their leaders have been “a snare at Mizpah, and a net spread on Tabor,” places that were probably centers of worship or political life, though the reason for naming them is uncertain. The LORD knows Ephraim fully, and nothing in Israel is hidden from him (5:3). Verse 4 states, “Their deeds won’t allow them to turn to their God,” a line both traditions read as a portrait of sin’s binding power; the site’s existing discussion at Deuteronomy 10:16 treats how a call to turn relates to God’s grace, and these notes point there rather than restating it. Pride testifies against Israel, and Judah stumbles too (5:5). The people come with flocks and herds to seek the LORD, but he has withdrawn himself (5:6). The prostitution and illegitimate children imagery (5:3–4, 7) is covenant language for unfaithfulness and is treated soberly here. Shared ground: both traditions read the passage as judgment on corrupt leadership and empty ritual, and both affirm that the LORD sees his people truly.

verses.text: “Listen to this, you priests! Listen, house of Israel, and give ear, house of the king! For the judgment is against you; for you have been a snare at Mizpah, and a net spread on Tabor.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD summons three groups: the priests, the house of Israel, and the house of the king. They have been “a snare at Mizpah, and a net spread on Tabor.” Arminian readers stress that leaders who should have guided the people instead trapped them, and that the judgment addresses those who used their influence for harm.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the hunting images as a picture of leadership that ensnares, and they note that judgment begins with those entrusted with authority. Shared ground: both traditions note that Mizpah and Tabor were probably sites of worship or political importance, though the exact reason for naming them is uncertain, and both read the verse as a charge against corrupt leadership.

verses.text: The rebels are deep in slaughter, but I discipline all of them.
verses.arminianNotes: “The rebels are deep in slaughter, but I discipline all of them.” The Hebrew of the first line is difficult, and the slaughter may refer to sacrifice or to violence. Arminian readers hear in “I discipline all of them” a correction meant to bring people back, not merely to destroy them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear God’s sovereign oversight: however deep the rebellion runs, the LORD is not distant, and his discipline reaches every rebel. Shared ground: both traditions acknowledge the difficulty of the first line, and both read the LORD’s discipline as purposeful, aimed at exposing sin and calling his people back to himself.

verses.text: I know Ephraim, and Israel is not hidden from me; for now, Ephraim, you have played the prostitute. Israel is defiled.
verses.arminianNotes: “I know Ephraim, and Israel is not hidden from me.” The LORD’s knowledge of Ephraim stands in contrast to the people’s lack of knowledge of him. Arminian readers stress that nothing escapes God’s sight, and that his knowledge here is that of a wronged covenant partner who sees the unfaithfulness clearly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize God’s exhaustive knowledge of his people, including their hidden sin, and see the declaration “Israel is defiled” as his authoritative verdict. Shared ground: both traditions affirm God’s complete knowledge, read the contrast with Israel’s failure to know the LORD as deliberate, and treat the prostitution language soberly as covenant unfaithfulness.

verses.text: Their deeds won’t allow them to turn to their God, for the spirit of prostitution is within them, and they don’t know the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: “Their deeds won’t allow them to turn to their God.” Arminian readers read this as the self-imposed bondage of habitual sin: repeated choices form a captivity from which people cannot free themselves. Only God’s grace can restore the capacity to turn, and many Arminians hold that this grace is extended to the people and can be received or refused.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as a clear statement of moral inability: “the spirit of prostitution is within them,” and they “don’t know the LORD,” so they cannot turn unless God renews the heart (compare Deuteronomy 30:6). Shared ground: both traditions agree that sin enslaves and that turning requires grace.

verses.text: The pride of Israel testifies to his face. Therefore Israel and Ephraim will stumble in their iniquity. Judah also will stumble with them.
verses.arminianNotes: “The pride of Israel testifies to his face.” Israel’s arrogance becomes a witness against him. Arminian readers see pride as the chosen posture that blocks repentance, and they note that Judah, which was warned in 4:15, “also will stumble with them.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see pride as the root of the inability described in verse 4, and the stumbling of Israel, Ephraim, and Judah as God’s just response. Shared ground: both traditions read pride as the obstacle to returning, and both note that Judah’s inclusion shows the warning of 4:15 went unheeded, at least in part. The same opening line recurs in 7:10.

verses.text: They will go with their flocks and with their herds to seek the LORD, but they won’t find him. He has withdrawn himself from them.
verses.arminianNotes: “They will go with their flocks and with their herds to seek the LORD, but they won’t find him.” Arminian readers stress that seeking God through sacrifice without changed hearts fails; the LORD’s withdrawal answers their unfaithfulness, though he still looks for genuine seeking (compare 5:15).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD’s withdrawal as his sovereign judgment: he is not at the disposal of worshipers who bring animals but not repentance. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as rejecting ritual detached from loyalty, a theme 6:6 makes explicit, and both see the withdrawal as purposeful, aimed at the earnest seeking described in 5:15.

verses.text: They are unfaithful to the LORD; for they have borne illegitimate children. Now the new moon will devour them with their fields.
verses.arminianNotes: “They are unfaithful to the LORD; for they have borne illegitimate children.” Arminian readers see the children as a picture of a generation raised outside covenant loyalty, the result of the parents’ choices. The line “Now the new moon will devour them” may mean that their festivals, or a short span of time, will bring judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the “illegitimate children” as a generation formed by idolatry rather than covenant teaching, and they see the new moon, likely a festival, turned from celebration into the occasion of judgment. Shared ground: both traditions read the imagery soberly as covenant unfaithfulness, acknowledge that the sense of “new moon” is uncertain, and see a religious calendar without loyalty as empty.
